content.text: If you have several conditions using `if` and `else if`, it’s often clearer to use a different construct known as `switch case`. Using this approach you write your condition once, then list all possible outcomes and what should happen for each of them.
To try this out, here’s a weather constant containing the string `sunny`:
We can use a `switch` block to print one of four different messages:

content.code:
switch weather {
case "rain":
  print("Bring an umbrella")
case "snow":
  print("Wrap up warm")
case "sunny":
  print("Wear sunscreen")
default:
  print("Enjoy your day!")
}

content.text: In that example, the last case – `default` – is required because Swift makes sure you cover all possible cases so that no eventuality is missed off. If the weather is anything other than rain, snow, or sun, the `default` case will be run.
Swift will only run the code inside each case. If you want execution to continue on to the next case, use the `fallthrough` keyword like this:

content.code:
switch weather {
case "rain":
  print("Bring an umbrella")
case "snow":
  print("Wrap up warm")
case "sunny":
  print("Wear sunscreen")
  fallthrough
default:
  print("Enjoy your day!")
}

title: Switch statements
question: Which of these statements are true about `switch case`?
hint: Swift takes the safety of your code seriously, which means it will make sure all possibilities are handled.

correct.answer: Switch statements are often clearer to read than multiple `if` conditions.
correct.reason: They help us by focusing on one specific check, rather than many possible checks.

correct.answer: Code from the following case will be run if you use `fallthrough`.
correct.reason: By default Swift will stop executing code in a switch block once it reaches the end of a case that was matched.

correct.answer: You must list all outcomes as `case` statements or use `default`.
correct.reason: Switch statements must be exhaustive in Swift, which means that all possible cases are catered for.

correct.answer: You place the value you want to check at the start.
correct.reason: Switch statements require some sort of value to check at the beginning.

correct.answer: The default case is written as `default:` rather than `case default:`.
correct.reason: You omit the `case` keyword for the default case.

correct.answer: If you want to match all other values, use `default`.
correct.reason: This acts as a catch-all for unmatched cases.

wrong.answer: Switch statements don't work with integers.
wrong.reason: Switch statements work just fine with integers.

wrong.answer: The default case is always needed.
wrong.reason: This default case is not needed if you already cover all other cases, such as with an enum.
You can use `fallthrough` as many times as you want.

wrong.answer: Switch statements work best with constants.
wrong.reason: Switch statements work just fine with variables.

wrong.answer: You can have a maximum of 10 cases.
wrong.reason: You may have as many cases as you want.

wrong.answer: Switch statements make your code run more slowly.
